Taking out private/retail hedge fund competitors. This feels exactly like the Retail Clearance event from Aug. 

Today a friend sent me this BofA Securities report while I was literally reading a front page article on Investing, warning retail investors of an impending "AI Monetization Failure." Citing BofA European Equity Strategist Sebastian Raedler, media outlets splashed quotes about falling token prices (-50% since summer) and slightly cooling U.S. business spending on AI as proof that the AI cycle is hitting a wall. 

Meanwhile, behind the paywall, Bank of America Securities published a completely different message for institutional clients and mega-fund managers.  "US Semiconductors State of the Union: High Utilization Keeps AI Cycle Structurally Resilient" 

Compare What BofA is Saying:
BofA Retail: "Token prices are collapsing, monetization is failing, AI cycle is over." 
BofA Institutions: "SOX already prices a crash we don't expect. Investors are paying post-crash multiples (~13x fwd PE) for a cycle that hasn't crashed."
BofA Retail: "Demand is fading and business spend is cooling off." 
BofA Institutions: "Full utilization, not dark fiber. Deployed AI runs near 100% capacity; older GPU rental rates are UP 12%–37% YTD (sign of scarcity, not glut)."
BofA Retail: "Warning sign of capital cycle failure." 
BofA Institutions: "Agentic AI, consumer (Meta Muse) & enterprise (OpenAI Dots/Spaces) will be the NEXT 10x+ demand wave."

Retail is being fooled into mistaking price-per-token deflation (caused by model optimization and competition) for lack of demand. 
In reality, infrastructure supply remains the binding constraint—hyperscalers and enterprises literally cannot get GPU compute and power fast enough.
Nvidia is already clocking ~$10B in 1H26 alone in Physical AI compute. The growth pipeline moves from Hopper (18bn/GW)toBlackwell(25bn) to Rubin ($40bn).

We saw this exact same "bubble bursting" and "demand decline" rumor cycle during the August Retail Clearance dip. Public headlines stoke fear out nothing, shake out weak retail hands, liquidate competitors, and lower entry valuations just ahead of earnings, so big money can load up on cheap positions.

note_tweet.text:
Privacy in the Age of AI - Is Privacy truly dead?

Unbelievable in less than a year we've gone from OpenClaw to now multiple personal AI agent platforms namely - Grokbot, OpenAI Dots, Meta Muse and Google Gemini/Spark just to name a few.

In order for these to be useful you need to feed it info, they are very data hungry and it's the "context" paired with the power of AI that makes them so useful.

But what happens when they start harvesting more data than what you thought?

Meta's Muse builds and maintains detailed “pages” or profiles on friends, family, colleagues, partners, and others mentioned in those communications—even people who never signed up for Muse or consented to any data sharing. These profiles can include relationship history, preferences, shared interests, and other details extracted from emails, chats, contacts, and photos. Muse is instructed to update them roughly hourly using the user’s data (plus public information).

I'd argue this extends surveillance to non-consenting third parties: your consent covers your data, but not the information about others sitting in your inbox or messages. Meta’s response is that this context is needed for the agent to be useful which is probably true.

Interestingly from my quick research, none of the other personal agent platforms go to this level of data harvesting. The cynic in me thinks this is what happens when your personal agent is built by a company who's business is to sell advertising. But the practical implication is Meta is right, the more data you give your personal agent the more useful it will be.

So what's it going to be?
